name: Vilon

lead: Vilon is a two-amino-acid peptide (lysine and glutamic acid) developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in St. Petersburg and described as an immune-system and anti-aging "bioregulator". People discuss it in longevity circles, with a looks payoff that is the hope of slower tissue ageing and a younger appearance.

Khavinson's group proposes that Vilon loosens condensed chromatin in ageing lymphocytes and so reactivates silenced genes, reported from cell cultures. Published work is mostly cell-culture and mouse experiments, including effects on tumour development and lifespan in mice, much of it from the originating institute. No controlled human trial of Vilon was found and no appearance effect is established.

paras: It is sold as a research peptide and discussed in short-course bioregulator routines in longevity communities. Any visible effect on appearance is a hope rather than a documented result.
No systematic human safety data were found. It is not an approved drug in the US or EU and is sold as a research peptide.

angle.text: Vilon is a Lys-Glu peptide from Khavinson's bioregulator program, discussed as an anti-aging candidate on the idea that it slows tissue ageing and so a younger look. Data come from cell and mouse studies; no human trials are known.

lead: Vilon is a synthetic dipeptide made of the amino acids lysine and glutamic acid (Lys-Glu). It was developed by the Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson and colleagues at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology as part of a program on short peptide "bioregulators" [1]. It is described as an immunomodulatory and geroprotective (anti-aging) candidate.

Published work on Vilon consists mainly of cell-culture and animal experiments, much of it from Khavinson's own group. Reported findings include effects on lymphocyte chromatin and on tumour development and lifespan in mice [1][2]. No controlled human trial of Vilon specifically was found, and it is not an approved medicine in the US or EU. It has no established link to facial appearance; its place in looksmaxxing discussion is as a longevity peptide.

paras: Vilon is a two-residue peptide, L-lysyl-L-glutamic acid, with a molecular weight of about 275 g/mol [1]. It belongs to a family of short peptides (di-, tri- and tetrapeptides) that Khavinson's group describes as bioregulators acting on gene expression; related entries include Epitalon [1].

According to an AI-generated encyclopedia summary, Khavinson's group moved in the 1980s and 1990s from extracting polypeptide complexes from animal organs (such as Thymalin) to synthesising short peptides, and Vilon was introduced as a synthetic immunomodulatory dipeptide in the late 1990s [1]. An early report in 2000 described subcutaneous Vilon inhibiting spontaneous tumour growth and increasing mean lifespan in mice [1].

The originating group proposes an epigenetic mechanism: in cultured lymphocytes from elderly donors, Vilon is reported to decondense facultative heterochromatin and activate ribosomal gene regions, with effects described as stronger in older cells [1]. These findings come largely from one research network, and the sources reviewed describe no independent replication in humans.

No studies found. Related animal work exists: in transgenic mice prone to mammary tumours, monthly injections of Vilon did not change tumour induction through 9 months, and the companion peptide Epitalon was the one associated with inhibited carcinogenesis later in life [2].
No systematic human safety data for Vilon were found. It is not approved as a drug in the US or EU and is available through research-peptide sellers.

timeline.event: Mouse study reports reduced spontaneous tumour growth and longer mean lifespan with Vilon [1].
Study in HER-2/neu transgenic mice compares Vilon and Epitalon for mammary tumour development [2].
